title: The frog in the well
hookLine: a frog who has never left his well meets a frog from the sea
carry: the sea is bigger than my well

lines: A FROG FROM THE SEA FALLS IN.
cards: A frog lives at the bottom of a well. He was born there, and he's done well for himself: he's fat, he's healthy, and he keeps the water clean of worms and bugs. One day another frog falls in.
This one comes from the sea. The well frog is curious, and a little suspicious. Where are you from?
The sea. And how big is the sea? Vivekananda told this story in Chicago, a few days into the Parliament, after speakers had been disagreeing.

teach.h: THE FROG LEAPS ACROSS HIS WELL.
teach.b: In his short talk called Why We Disagree, he lets the story play out. Is the sea as big as my well? the frog asks, and he leaps from one side of the well to the other. Bigger, says the sea frog.
A bigger leap. This big? Much bigger.
You can't compare the sea with your well.
So the well frog decides the visitor must be lying. Nothing can be bigger than my well, he says. Throw him out.
Here's the turn. Vivekananda doesn't point the story at any one group in the hall.
He puts himself in it first: he's a Hindu, he says, sitting in his own little well and thinking the whole world is that well. Then he names the others the same way.
Each of us is sitting in a little well and taking it for the world. He even thanks his American hosts for trying to break down the walls of those little worlds. That's the gentleness in it.
The joke isn't on the frog for living in a well. Everyone has to live somewhere, and this frog keeps his water clean. The trouble starts only at one sentence: nothing can be bigger than my well.
Underneath the joke is a Hindu teaching: the truth is bigger than any one view of it.
An old Rig Veda line, much quoted by Hindus, says it plainly: truth is one; the wise call it by many names. So humility about your own well isn't weakness in a Hindu; it's taking the sea seriously.
Not that anyone leaves home, but that no one throws out the visitor who says the water goes farther than they've seen.

how: Vivekananda's frog in the well is retold in Hindu talks, interfaith gatherings and school lessons as a picture of a narrow view, with the speaker himself counted among the frogs.

o: a teacher who urged every listener to leave home
a monk who told the frog story to mock other faiths
the monk who said he sat in his own little well too

games.q: the frog in the well — tap the pairs.
p: says the sea is far bigger
I'm in my own little well too

s: Vivekananda told the frog story to mock other religions
he put himself in a well first, then named every group the same way.
the well frog measured the sea by leaping across his well
each leap bigger, and still the sea frog said: much bigger.
the story ends with the well frog moving to the sea
he decides the visitor is lying and wants him thrown out.

games.q: you're the well frog. a stranger says the sea is far bigger than your well, bigger than any leap. what do you do?
o: decide he's lying and throw him out.
admit you've never thought about it.
games.why: the well frog throws him out. Vivekananda's twist: he says he's that frog too, and so is everyone sitting in the hall.

practice: Bring to mind your own well: the neighborhood, the family, the group or the way of seeing you grew up inside, and notice what's good about it, the water you keep clean.

Then remember one time someone told you the world was bigger than that, and you didn't want to hear it. No judging; just breathe there, and notice the frog's leap, measuring the sea against the walls.

wordCard.voice: Vivekananda. The monk who told the Chicago Parliament he was a frog in his own well, too.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the frog in the well, a saying for someone who takes their small world for the whole.

carryVoice: Your line: the sea is bigger than my well. Even mine, he said. Tomorrow, a teacher who said: not compassion, but service. Day nine hundred forty-one, done.
